evidence_quotes.quote: El presente estudio tiene como objetivo general identificar los factores que dificultan el acceso, la cobertura y la calidad de los servicios de agua y saneamiento en el distrito de Aguas Verdes, región Tumbes, y determinar si estos servicios se brindan con igualdad de derechos y respeto al medio ambiente.

La alta tasa de conexiones inactivas responde principalmente a la escasez del servicio, originada por las deficiencias en la infraestructura relacionada con los sistemas de bombeo, almacenamiento y distribución.

La información obtenida es el resultado de la encuesta tomada a una muestra de 94 pobladores del distrito de Aguas Verdes, realizada en el mes de junio del 2021; así como, entrevistas a funcionarios y revisión de documentación de la UESST, y del resultado del taller participativo de dirigentes comunales.

El resultado indica que el 23% de la población no dispone de una conexión de agua potable a través de la red pública, mientras que el 32% carece de un sistema de alcantarillado. En consecuencia, el 77% de la población cuenta con una conexión domiciliaria de agua potable y el 68% dispone de acceso a una red de alcantarillado.

Sin embargo, en las entrevistas a los funcionarios de la UESST, se tiene como resultado que, de la población que cuenta con conexión (77%), el 67.3% tiene conexión activa y el 32.7% no tiene conexión activa, por lo que en consecuencia solo el 51.8% cuenta con servicio efectivo de agua potable, con una continuidad de solo 2 horas diarias en promedio y en algunos sectores Inter diario.

En el caso de la presente investigación, la población del distrito de Aguas Verdes, en la encuesta manifestó que el mal estado de los servicios de saneamiento y obras, se debe en parte a factores de corrupción de los funcionarios de las entidades públicas vinculadas a dichos servicios.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household drinking-water and sewerage/sanitation service access, active versus inactive domestic connections, and supply continuity in the urban district of Aguas Verdes (Zarumilla province, Tumbes region, Peru).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the thesis touches on broad institutional and governance issues (operational management weaknesses of UESST and the municipality MDAV, lack of citizen participation in proposing civil works, political interference, perceived corruption in public-works procurement, and a brief interview observation that SUNASS had not conducted supervision/sanctions by 2021). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification, however, c2 is NO: the study does not empirically examine any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, disconnection rules, discretion/accommodation, or utility ownership/regulatory structure governing access). Inactive connections (32.7%) and poor continuity (1-2 hours/day) are explicitly attributed to physical water-source scarcity and 40-50-year-old deteriorated pumping/pipe infrastructure; tariff theory (Section 4.1) and the 2005-2018 concession / 2018 OTASS takeover (Section 3.3) appear only as literature or historical background and are not empirically analyzed in relation to household access, while the empirical governance findings concern generic civil-works project delivery, sanitary education, and macro-governance/procurement corruption perceptions.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary mixed-methods empirical data: a probabilistic household/resident survey in Aguas Verdes (reported sample calculation n = 94 in June 2021, with n = 95 responses in most tables), semi-structured interviews with 8 UESST officials, 1 MDAV official, and 2 ODS-Tumbes/SUNASS officials, a February 2020 participatory workshop, and institutional document review.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete household access and service availability outcomes, including formal drinking-water connection coverage (77%), sewerage connection coverage (68%), active/effective water connection coverage (67.3% of connections active, yielding 51.8% effective coverage), supply continuity (1-2 hours per day or inter-daily), and resident satisfaction with supply frequency.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (households/residents of Aguas Verdes district, universe 4,000 families; survey sample n = 94/95, plus key institutional informants), study design (cross-sectional mixed-methods descriptive case study), and access outcomes are clearly identifiable. The paper's examined explanatory factors (water-source shortage, aged infrastructure, municipal civil-works execution, and perceived procurement corruption) are identifiable as descriptive diagnostics, though they fail Criterion 2's rule-type exposure scope.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in Spanish (with an English abstract on PDF Page 5). Although Spanish is outside the automatic no-translation list in Criterion 9 (English, Portuguese, Dutch), direct full-text translation/assessment from the provided text is feasible per Criterion 10.

study_design: Mixed-methods cross-sectional descriptive case study (resident survey, semi-structured key-informant interviews, participatory workshop, and document review)
population_and_sample: Households/residents of Aguas Verdes district, Zarumilla province, Tumbes region, Peru (universe: 4,000 families / 16,000-18,946 inhabitants; survey sample calculated as n = 94, with n = 95 responses reported in most tables), plus 11 institutional officials interviewed (8 UESST, 1 MDAV, 2 ODS-Tumbes/SUNASS) and participatory workshop attendees
exposure: Physical water-source scarcity, aged water/sewerage infrastructure, municipal civil-works project execution, operational maintenance, and general perceptions of corruption and weak public management (no rule-type legal or regulatory mechanism governing household access analyzed)
outcome: Household drinking-water connection coverage (77%), sewerage connection coverage (68%), effective/active water service coverage (51.8%), supply continuity (1-2 hours/day), and user satisfaction with service frequency and sewerage maintenance
rationale: Exclude under E03 (Wrong exposure). While this Peruvian Master's thesis in Social Management empirically documents household water and sewerage coverage, active connection rates, and service continuity in Aguas Verdes (satisfying c1, c3, and c4), it fails Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification. Rather than analyzing a legal, administrative, or regulatory rule directly governing household service access (such as eligibility/tenure requirements, administrative burdens, tariff/disconnection rules, or utility ownership/regulatory rules linked to access), the empirical analysis attributes service deficits and inactive connections to physical water-source scarcity and deteriorated 40-50-year-old infrastructure, alongside generic civil-works project delivery, lack of sanitary education, and broad perceptions of corruption in public-works procurement.
